summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to estimate and price fabrication and welding jobs. You will gather the information and visit the site, take off quantities and plan cutting from stock lengths, estimate labour, consumables and other direct costs, add overheads, contingency and profit, and show GCT correctly. You will also write and present a professional quotation, handle variations, check estimates and review the real costs after the job.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). An **estimate** works out what a job will cost and what to charge for it. A good estimate wins work at a price that pays every cost and leaves a fair profit. A careless one either loses the job to a competitor or wins it at a loss. In a small fabrication shop the estimator is often the owner or a senior welder, so Level 3 trainees are expected to measure, take off quantities, estimate labour and help build the price.

You will price the kind of work Jamaican shops quote for every week: gates, grilles, railings, staircases, carports, tank stands, trailers and small structural frames. All money is in Jamaican dollars (J$); sizes are metric.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders and fabricators who price jobs or help their supervisor to price them.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Find out what the client wants; get or make a drawing; visit and measure the site; note access, fixings and hazards.
List every material and amount from the drawing; write a cutting list; plan cutting from stock lengths; work out masses, areas and waste.
Break the job into tasks, estimate the hours for each from records and experience, and price them at the right labour rate.
Consumables, hardware, finishes, subcontract work, transport and equipment hire.
Add overheads, contingency and profit (mark-up or margin), then show GCT at the current rate.
Set out the scope, price, exclusions, validity and terms clearly and professionally, and explain it to the client.
Have the figures checked; price variations in writing; compare the actual costs with the estimate after the job.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on estimates and quotations, quantities, calculations, labour, costs, pricing, risk, suppliers, checking, variations and professional practice.
A **written paper** with short answers (many are calculations: masses, costs, mark-ups, deposits, areas) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two team practicals**: measuring a real door or window opening and taking off the materials for a grille or gate (sketch, cutting list, stock lengths, mass, hardware, paint); and pricing that job on an estimate sheet, writing the quotation and presenting it to a 'client' in a role play, including pricing a variation.

blocks.note: Bring a calculator to every session and show your working. Most marks are lost on units (millimetres and metres, kilograms and tonnes) and on percentages worked from the wrong figure.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Estimates, quotations and the estimating process

head: Term
What it is
Notes
rows: A reasoned forecast of what the job will cost and its likely price
A guide: the final price may change when the details are known.
A firm offer to do the stated work for the stated price, open for a stated time
Once the client accepts it in time, both sides are bound by it.
A formal bid, usually in competition, on the client's own forms and rules

flow: Take the enquiry: what the client wants, sizes, finish, budget and when it is needed
Visit the site: measure, check fixings, access and hazards, take photos
Make or check a drawing and agree it with the client
Take off quantities and write the cutting list
Get prices from suppliers and subcontractors
Estimate the labour hours, task by task
Add consumables, hardware, finishes, transport and hire
Add overheads, contingency and profit; then GCT
Have a second person check the figures
Write the quotation, send or present it, and follow it up

ul: **Drawings and specification:** sizes, sections, material grade, finish (paint, galvanising, stainless steel), welding and fixing details.
**Quantities:** how many of each item.
**Site details:** what the job is fixed to, access for delivery, power on site, working at height, working hours allowed.
**Dates:** when the client needs it, and any time the site is closed.
**Who supplies what:** for example who builds the concrete footings, who wires an automatic gate motor.

head: Check
Why it matters
rows: Measure each opening at the top, middle and bottom, and both sides; check the diagonals
Openings are rarely square; the smallest size decides whether the job fits.
Decides the fixings (expansion bolts, chemical anchors, cast-in plates, footings) and their cost.
A narrow lane, steps or a steep road may need a smaller truck, more trips, extra hands or a crane.
No power means a generator for site welding and drilling.
Overhead lines, working at height, fragile roofs, traffic, the public: each needs a control, and some cost money.
Sea air and salt spray near the coast attack steel fast; the finish may need to be galvanising or a better paint system.
Photos with a tape in view
A record of the conditions and sizes for the estimator and the team.

blocks.note: Most structural steel used in Jamaica is imported and its price follows world prices and the exchange rate with the US dollar. Prices can move between the day you quote and the day you buy. The hurricane season (1 June to 30 November) and the heavy rains can also delay site work. A good estimate allows for both.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Quantities: take-off, cutting lists and stock lengths

ul: Always use the **written dimensions**. Measure from the drawing only when a size is missing, and then confirm it with the client or designer.
On a scale drawing, real size = drawing size × the scale number. At 1:20, a frame drawn 62 mm long is 62 × 20 = **1240 mm** long.
Keep units the same through every calculation: work lengths in metres for pricing, and in millimetres for cutting lists.

blocks.p: A **quantity take-off** is a list of every material and how much of it the job needs, taken from the drawings. Group it by type: each steel section by size (total length), plate by thickness (area or number of sheets), hardware by count, finishes by area, fixings by count.

Steel sections usually come in fixed stock lengths, often 6 m (about 20 ft); check with the supplier. Sheet often comes as 2440 mm × 1220 mm (8 ft × 4 ft). You must buy whole lengths and sheets, so plan the cutting before you count what to buy.

flow: List the pieces, longest first
Fit pieces into each stock length, allowing a saw cut (about 3 mm) for each piece
Start a new length when the next piece will not fit
Note the offcuts; keep only those long enough to be used on another job
Count the stock lengths and work out what is bought

blocks.p: Example: the stiles and rails above in 6 m lengths. Length 1: 1900 + 1900 + 1050 + 1050 = 5900 mm, plus 4 cuts × 3 mm = 5912 mm, leaving an 88 mm scrap end. Length 2: the third rail, 1050 mm, leaving a 4.94 m offcut. So **2 lengths (12 m)** are bought for 6.95 m of parts. Unless that offcut is really used on another job, the job carries the cost of both full lengths.

blocks.note: Dividing the total length by the stock length gives only the least number of lengths possible. Pieces cannot be joined unless the drawing allows it, and every cut takes a few millimetres, so a cutting plan often needs one more length than the simple division says.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **waste allowance** is added to material quantities to cover offcuts too short to use, cutting losses, mistakes and damaged material. Where you have made a full cutting plan, the offcuts are already counted and only a small allowance is needed. Without a plan, many shops add about 5 to 10% for sections, and more for plate cut into shapes. The business's own past jobs are the best guide.
Adding a percentage: new amount = amount × (1 + percentage ÷ 100). J$64,000 of steel with 8% waste: 64,000 × 1.08 = **J$69,120**.

Steel has a density of about **7850 kg per cubic metre**. Mass matters because steel is often priced by the kilogram or tonne, galvanisers charge by the kilogram, and transport and lifting depend on it.

ul: **Plate:** mass (kg) = length (m) × width (m) × thickness (mm) × 7.85. A plate 1.5 m × 1.0 m × 8 mm = 1.5 × 1.0 × 8 × 7.85 = **94.2 kg**.
**Sections:** use the supplier's section table, which gives the mass in **kg/m** (kilograms per metre). Mass = total length × kg/m.

**Working it out yourself:** kg/m = cross-section area (mm²) × 0.00785. Flat bar 50 × 6 mm: 300 mm² × 0.00785 = 2.36 kg/m. Square bar 12 mm: 144 mm² × 0.00785 = 1.13 kg/m. Round bar 16 mm: π × 8² = 201 mm², so 1.58 kg/m.
1 tonne (t) = 1000 kg.
Sheet and plate: length × width for each side painted. A sheet painted on both sides has twice its area to cover.
Tube and bar: outside perimeter × length. 40 mm square tube has a perimeter of 0.16 m, so each metre has 0.16 m² of surface.
Paint needed (litres) = area × number of coats ÷ the spreading rate on the tin (m² per litre), plus an allowance for losses (larger for spraying than for brushing).

blocks.p: Example: 20 m² to be painted with 2 coats at 10 m² per litre, with 15% for losses: 20 × 2 ÷ 10 = 4 litres; 4 × 1.15 = 4.6 litres. Round up to whole tins: one gallon (about 3.8 L) and one quart (about 0.95 L) give 4.7 litres.

ul: Circumference = π × diameter. A ring of 750 mm diameter needs 3.142 × 750 = 2357 mm of bar on its centre line.
Area of a circle = π × radius². A round plate 800 mm across has an area of 3.142 × 0.4² = 0.503 m².

blocks.p: Labour is often the biggest cost on a fabrication job and the hardest to estimate. The best method is to **break the job into tasks** and estimate each one, then add them up.

head: Task (pair of driveway gates)
People
Hours each
Person-hours
rows: Read the drawing and set out

blocks.p: The person-hours add up to **44.5**. At a labour rate of J$1,400 an hour: 44.5 × 1,400 = **J$62,300**. A **person-hour** is one person working for one hour: two people working five hours is 10 person-hours, even though the job takes five hours on the clock.

ul: **Records of past jobs:** time sheets from similar jobs show how long the work really took. They are the most reliable source.
**Standard times or rates** the shop uses: for example minutes per metre of weld, per cut or per hole.
**Experience,** checked against the records.
A **sense check**: compare the total with a similar job, or with a rate per kilogram or per metre from past jobs.

blocks.h: Welding is only part of the time

blocks.p: A welder's arc is on for only part of the day. The rest goes on handling, fitting, chipping slag, changing electrodes, grinding, moving the work and checking. The share of time the arc is actually on (the **operating factor**) is often only about 20 to 30% for stick welding and somewhat higher for MIG; it varies with the job and the shop.

Example: 18 m of fillet weld at a travel speed of about 0.15 m a minute is 18 ÷ 0.15 = 120 minutes (2 hours) of arc time. With an operating factor of 25%, the welder needs about 2 ÷ 0.25 = **8 hours**. If only the 2 hours of arc time were priced, the job would lose money.

blocks.note: Do not forget: setting out, handling heavy parts, machine set-up, cleaning up, inspection, loading, travelling to site, fixing, and making good after fixing. These are the hours most often left out.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The labour rate charged must cover more than the basic hourly wage. It must also cover the employer's statutory payroll contributions (such as NIS, NHT, Education Tax and the HEART/NSTA Trust contribution), holiday and sick pay, and time that cannot be charged to any job. Some shops also put a share of overheads into one 'charge-out rate'; others add overheads separately. Either way works, as long as the overheads are counted once and only once.

ul: Heat: hard work in the midday sun is slower, and the team needs rest breaks and water.
Rain and the hurricane season can stop site work.
Access, working at height and work around occupied homes, schools or hotels are slower than workshop work.
Travel time to and from site is paid time.

sections.title: Consumables, equipment and other direct costs

blocks.h: Weld metal and electrodes or wire

flow: List the welds from the drawing by type and size, and add up the length of each
Work out the cross-section of each weld: for an equal-leg fillet with a flat face it is leg × leg ÷ 2
Volume = cross-section × length; mass = volume × 7.85 g per cm³
Divide by the deposit efficiency to get the mass of electrode or wire to buy
Round up to whole packets or spools

blocks.p: Example: 40 m of 4 mm fillet. Cross-section = 4 × 4 ÷ 2 = 8 mm². Volume = 8 × 40 000 mm = 320 000 mm³ = 320 cm³. Mass = 320 × 7.85 = 2512 g, about **2.5 kg of weld metal**. Real welds are a little convex, so add a small allowance.

head: Process
Typical deposit efficiency
Why
rows: Stubs thrown away, flux turned into slag, spatter

blocks.p: For the 2.5 kg above: with stick electrodes at about 60%, 2.5 ÷ 0.6 = 4.2 kg, so one 5 kg packet. With MIG wire at about 90%, 2.5 ÷ 0.9 = 2.8 kg.

blocks.note: These efficiencies are typical figures; electrode makers and the shop's own records give better ones. Always price whole packets or spools, and remember that opened low-hydrogen electrodes that are not kept dry are wasted.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Gas used = flow rate × arc time. At 14 litres a minute for 3 hours (180 minutes) of arc time: 14 × 180 = 2520 litres, plus an allowance for purging and leaks. Find how many litres your cylinder holds (on its label or from the supplier), and price the share used or the cylinder rental, as the shop does. Another way is a cost per arc hour from past jobs.

ul: Grinding, flap and cutting discs, wire brushes, drill bits, saw blades, oxy-fuel gases, marking materials.
These are priced from past jobs (for example discs per metre of weld or per tonne of steel) or as a small percentage of labour.
**Hardware:** hinges, drop bolts, locks, latches, rollers and tracks, bolts and anchors. Count each item from the drawing.
**Finishes:** primer, paint and thinners from the area; or hot-dip galvanising, which galvanisers usually price by the kilogram.

**Subcontract work** such as galvanising, machining, powder coating, concrete footings or electrical work: get the subcontractor's written price, then add the cost of handling, transport both ways, the time it adds to the job, and the business's mark-up if it carries the risk.

blocks.note: Hot-dip galvanising needs vent and drain holes in closed hollow sections, so zinc can flow in and out and trapped air cannot burst the section. Allow for drilling them, and for the steel being away for some days.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Transport:** truck hire or vehicle costs, fuel, the number of trips, loading and unloading time.
**Equipment hire:** crane, scaffold, mobile work platform, generator. Price the whole hire: delivery and collection, the operator, the minimum hire period and any standing time.
Transport and fixing on site, with the fixings (bolts, anchors, concrete)
Making good after fixing (filling holes, touching up paint)
Removing and disposing of old work
Hardware and finishes
Subcontract handling and delays
Travel time and site set-up

head: Type of cost
Meaning
Workshop examples
rows: Costs that belong to this one job and would not be spent without it
Steel, hardware and paint for this gate; the hours worked on it; electrodes and discs used on it; transport and crane hire for it
Running costs of the business, shared by all jobs
Workshop rent, JPS electricity, water, insurance, phone and internet, office costs, vehicle costs not charged to a job, wear of machines, the owner's admin time

blocks.p: A share of the overheads is added to every job. A common way is an **overhead rate per labour hour**: yearly overheads ÷ yearly productive hours. Example: overheads of J$3,600,000 a year; four workers each with about 1,500 productive hours a year give 6,000 hours; 3,600,000 ÷ 6,000 = **J$600 per hour**. A job of 44.5 hours then carries 44.5 × 600 = J$26,700 of overheads. Other shops add overheads as a percentage of direct costs.

A **contingency** is an amount added to cover known risks that cannot be priced exactly: rotten fixings found when old grilles come out, a steel price rise, extra trips on a difficult site. It is set by how risky the job is, often a few per cent. It is not hidden profit; if the risk does not happen, the money is part of the job's result.

head: Point
Mark-up
Margin
rows: Profit as a percentage of the **cost**
Profit as a percentage of the **selling price**

blocks.p: Worked example: a job costs J$240,000. With a **30% mark-up**, the profit is 240,000 × 0.30 = J$72,000 and the price is J$312,000. The margin on that price is 72,000 ÷ 312,000 = **23.1%**, not 30%. If the owner wants a **25% margin**, the price is 240,000 ÷ 0.75 = J$320,000, a profit of J$80,000 (a mark-up of 33.3%).

blocks.note: Mixing up mark-up and margin makes every job earn less than planned. Always ask which one the business uses, and check the result: profit ÷ price should give the margin you meant.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **General Consumption Tax (GCT)** is the tax added to the price of most goods and services in Jamaica. A business registered for GCT must charge it.

Add GCT **after** profit, on the price before tax, and show it as **its own line** on the quotation, at the current rate. Check the current rate with Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) or the business's accountant; never copy the rate from an old quotation.
A business registered for GCT can usually claim back the GCT it pays on materials, so materials are usually priced before GCT. Ask how your business handles this.

head: Line
Example: pair of driveway gates (J$)
rows: Worked out on 256,600 and shown separately

blocks.h: Unit rates: quick prices and checks

blocks.p: Simple, repeated items are often priced by a **unit rate** from past jobs: per metre of handrail, per square metre of grille, or per kilogram of fabricated steel. At J$5,200 per metre, 12 m of handrail is 12 × 5,200 = J$62,400. Unit rates are also a quick sense check on a full estimate, but a rate is only as good as the jobs it came from: a difficult site or an unusual design needs a full estimate.
Remember: **profit = price − cost**. A job priced at J$150,000 that costs J$118,000 makes J$32,000 profit.

Many fabricators ask for a **deposit** before starting: it pays for the materials and confirms that the client is serious. Larger jobs often have stage payments (for example on delivery) and the balance on completion. Agree the terms in writing. A deposit is worked out as a percentage of the agreed price: 35% of J$180,000 is J$63,000.

head: The quotation should include
Why
rows: Business name, address, contact details, date and a quotation number
So it can be identified and referred to
The client's name and the site address
So it is clear who it is for and where the work is
The scope: description, drawing reference, sizes, materials and finish
So both sides agree exactly what is included
To show what the price does not cover, and avoid arguments later
The price, with GCT on its own line at the current rate
So the client knows the full cost
Material prices and exchange rates change
So cash comes in as costs are paid out
Time to complete, and what it depends on
So the client can plan, and delays caused by others are not the shop's fault
So extra work is agreed before it is done
Shows what the business stands behind
A place for the client to sign and date
Turns acceptance into a clear agreement

blocks.p: Typical exclusions on fabrication quotations: building or masonry work; concrete footings; electrical connections for automatic gates; removing and disposing of old work; permits; repainting walls after fixing. If the client or another trade must do something before you can fix (for example build footings to a size and by a date), say so in the quotation.

blocks.h: Protecting the business from price changes

ul: Give a short validity period when prices are moving.
On a long job, include a **price-change clause**: the price may be adjusted if steel prices or the exchange rate change by more than a stated amount before the steel is bought.
Buy the steel as soon as the order and deposit are received.
If a client accepts after the validity has run out, re-check the prices and confirm or revise the price in writing before starting.
Be honest and clear. Price the work the drawing and specification ask for.

If the client wants a lower price, offer a **priced alternative** openly (for example painted instead of galvanised, or a simpler design) and explain what the client gives up. Never quietly use thinner steel or cheaper materials than quoted.
If a client asks how the price is made up, explain the main parts (materials, labour, finishing, fixing), but keep your suppliers' trade prices and discounts confidential.
If a competitor is cheaper, check your own costs, then explain the value you offer honestly. Never run down a competitor.
Get suppliers' prices in writing, from more than one supplier where you can, and compare price, quality and delivery time.

flow: Prepare: know the drawing, the price and the options
Walk the client through the scope and what is excluded
Explain the price, the payment terms, validity and timing
Listen to questions and note any changes asked for
Price any change in writing; do not agree new prices on the spot
Follow up in writing, and keep a copy on the job file

blocks.note: Neat, accurate quotations win work. Use the business's letterhead or template, check spelling and figures, and keep the language plain. Clients in Jamaica often compare three quotations, so make yours easy to read and complete.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Checking, variations and reviewing the job

ul: A **second person** checks the figures before the quotation goes out. People rarely spot their own errors.
Check the quantities against the drawing: every part, the right number off.
Check the units: millimetres or metres, kilograms or tonnes, hours or days.
Check that every price is current and for the right specification (for example 6 mm plate, not 5 mm).
Check that nothing is missing: use a checklist of cost headings.
Do a **sense check**: compare the total with a similar past job, per kilogram or per metre.

head: Common estimating error
How to avoid it
rows: Wrong unit (1240 m typed for 1240 mm)
Write the unit on every line; sense-check each total
Mark-up used where margin was meant
State which is used; check profit ÷ price
Check each supplier price against the specification
Transport, fixing or finishing left out
Spreadsheet formula pointing to the wrong cell
Test the sheet with simple numbers; lock formula cells; check totals by hand

blocks.p: A **spreadsheet** is useful because formulas update every total when a figure changes. But it does not check itself: a wrong formula gives wrong answers very neatly. Keep a tested template, protect the formula cells, and still check the main totals by hand.
A **variation** is a change to the agreed work asked for after the price has been agreed: extra work, less work or different work.

flow: Make sure you understand exactly what the client wants
Explain that it is a change to the agreed job and will be priced
Measure and price it the same way as the main job
Send a written variation: the work, the extra (or reduced) price, GCT at the current rate, and any change to the completion date
Get the client's signed approval before doing the work
Update the job plan, order materials, tell the team, keep it on the job file

blocks.note: Do not do extra work on a promise to 'just add it to the bill'. Without an agreed price in writing, the client may refuse to pay or dispute the amount when the final bill arrives.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: After the job, compare the **actual costs** with the estimate. This shows whether the job made the planned profit, and it makes the next estimate more accurate.

flow: Collect the real figures: supplier invoices, stock used, time sheets, subcontract bills, transport and hire
Set them beside the estimate, heading by heading
Work out each difference in J$ and as a percentage of the estimate
Find the reason for each large difference
Write down the lessons learned and update the rates and records

blocks.p: Example: labour was estimated at 60 hours and took 72 hours. The difference is 12 hours, and 12 ÷ 60 = **20% over** the estimate. The reason (for example rework after a cutting error, or a task that was missed) tells you what to change next time.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain the difference between an estimate, a quotation and a tender.
I can list the information needed to estimate a job and plan a site visit.
I can read sizes from a scale drawing.
I can do a quantity take-off and write a cutting list.
I can plan cuts from stock lengths and work out how many lengths to buy.
I can add a waste allowance and work out percentages correctly.
I can work out the mass of plate and sections, and the area to be painted.
I can break a job into tasks and estimate the labour hours and cost.
I can explain why welding time alone is not enough.
I can estimate electrodes or wire, gas and other consumables.
I can price hardware, finishes, subcontract work, transport and hire.
I can explain direct costs, overheads, contingency and profit, with examples.
I can work out an overhead rate per hour.
I can work out mark-up and margin, and convert one to the other.
I can show GCT correctly on a quotation.
I can write a complete, professional quotation with exclusions, validity and terms.
I can explain how to protect a price against rising costs.
I can check an estimate and spot common errors.

terms: Contingency
An amount added to cover known risks that cannot be priced exactly
Cutting list
A list of every piece to be cut, with its length and how many are needed
Cutting plan
A plan of which pieces are cut from each stock length or sheet
Deposit
Part of the price paid before work starts
Deposit efficiency
The share of the electrode or wire bought that ends up as weld metal
Direct cost
A cost that belongs to one job, such as its materials and labour
Estimate
A reasoned forecast of the cost and likely price of a job
Exclusions
Items stated in the quotation as not covered by the price
GCT
General Consumption Tax, added to the price at the current rate and shown separately
kg/m
Kilograms per metre: the mass of one metre of a steel section
Labour rate
The hourly amount charged for labour, covering wages and the employer's on-costs
Margin
Profit as a percentage of the selling price
Mark-up
Profit as a percentage of the cost
Operating factor
The share of a welder's time that the arc is actually on
Overheads
The running costs of the business, shared across all jobs
Person-hour
One person working for one hour
Price-change clause
A term allowing the price to change if material costs or exchange rates move
Quantity take-off
A list of all the materials and amounts needed, taken from the drawings
Quotation
A firm offer to do stated work for a stated price, open for a stated time
Stock length
The standard length in which a section is sold, often 6 m
Subcontractor
Another firm paid to do part of the job, such as galvanising
Tender
A formal, usually competitive bid made on the client's own forms
Validity
How long the quoted price stays open
Variation
A change to the agreed work, priced and approved before it is done
Waste allowance
Extra material added to cover offcuts, cutting losses and errors

c1.title: Window grilles in Bog Walk
c1.text: Tavia has measured five windows at a house in Bog Walk, St Catherine, for burglar-bar grilles. Each grille has a frame of 25 mm × 25 mm angle and seven upright bars of 12 mm square bar, each bar cut 1000 mm long. The frame angle for all five grilles needs four 6 m lengths, from a cutting plan that uses 22.4 m. Steel is sold in 6 m lengths.

c2.title: A carport in Portmore
c2.text: Rushane is estimating a steel carport for a house in Portmore, St Catherine. The posts will be bolted to concrete footings that the client's own mason will build. His task list is: marking and cutting 7 h, fitting and tacking 9 h, welding 12 h, grinding and cleaning 5 h, painting 8 h, and loading, transport and erection by 2 workers for 7 h each. The labour rate is J$1,450 an hour, although the welders' basic pay is J$1,100 an hour. The drawing shows about 30 m of 5 mm fillet welds.

c3.title: A tank stand for a school in Christiana
c3.text: Nordia is pricing a 4 m high steel stand for two water tanks at a primary school in Christiana, Manchester. The steel will be hot-dip galvanised by another firm in Kingston, well over 100 km away. Nobody yet knows whether the school's old concrete base is level and strong enough. The steel is imported and priced in US dollars. Her quotation is valid for 30 days, but the school board accepts it after six weeks.

c4.title: An outside staircase in Negril
c4.text: Kimoy has costed an outside steel staircase for a guest house in Negril, Westmoreland. The total cost, including overheads and contingency, is J$480,000, and the owner of her business wants a margin of 20% on the selling price. The design is hot-dip galvanised because the guest house is close to the sea. The guest house manager says the price is more than she budgeted for. The job will take about three weeks.

c5.title: A wider gate in Yallahs
c5.text: Leroy's team is halfway through making a sliding gate for a client in Yallahs, St Thomas, to a quotation the client signed. On a visit to the shop, the client asks for the gate to be made 600 mm wider and to have an automatic motor fitted, and says: "Just add it to the bill."

c6.title: Reviewing a trailer job in Falmouth
c6.text: After finishing a boat trailer for a fisherman in Falmouth, Trelawny, Jodian compares the actual costs with her estimate. Materials: estimated J$96,000, actual J$104,000, because the steel price rose before she ordered it. Labour: estimated 40 hours, actual 50 hours, because two parts were cut to the wrong length and made again. Consumables: estimated J$9,000, actual J$8,500.

questions.q: How many 6 m lengths of 12 mm square bar must be bought for the 35 upright bars?
o: 6 lengths
5 lengths
7 lengths
8 lengths
questions.why: Six 1000 mm bars would use the whole 6 m with nothing left for the saw cuts, so each length gives only five bars. 35 ÷ 5 = 7 lengths. Dividing 35 m by 6 m (5.8, so 6) ignores the cuts.

questions.q: Why should Tavia price the full 24 m of angle bought, not just the 22.4 m in her cutting plan?
o: The shop must buy whole lengths, so the offcuts are a cost of this job
The extra 1.6 m will be added to the grilles to make them stronger
Pricing more steel than is needed makes the quotation look more thorough
The client will be given all the offcuts to keep when the job is done
questions.why: Steel is sold in whole lengths, and offcuts too short to use on another job are paid for but wasted. Unless an offcut is really used elsewhere, this job carries its cost.

questions.q: The grilles have about 4 m² of surface, need 2 coats of primer, and the primer covers about 10 m² per litre. Allowing 20% for brush losses, how much primer is needed?
o: About 0.40 litres
About 0.80 litres
About 1.60 litres
About 0.96 litres
questions.why: 4 m² × 2 coats = 8 m² of coating; 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8 litres; with 20% for losses, 0.8 × 1.2 = 0.96 litres, so one 1 litre tin.

questions.q: What is the labour cost of Rushane's carport?
questions.why: The workshop tasks add up to 41 hours, and erection is 2 workers × 7 hours = 14 person-hours, so 55 person-hours × J$1,450 = J$79,750. Counting erection as only 7 hours gives J$69,600.

questions.q: About what mass of weld metal is in the 30 m of 5 mm fillet? (Cross-section about 12.5 mm²; steel about 7.85 g per cm³)
o: About 0.29 kg
About 2.9 kg
About 29 kg
About 4.9 kg
questions.why: 12.5 mm² × 30 000 mm = 375 000 mm³ = 375 cm³, and 375 × 7.85 = 2944 g, about 2.9 kg. About 4.9 kg is the mass of stick electrodes he might buy at 60% efficiency, not the weld metal.

questions.q: How should the client's own footings be dealt with in Rushane's quotation?
o: Leave them out of the quotation altogether, as they are not part of the steelwork
Price them as extra labour hours in case the mason does not turn up
Include them in the price, and pay the mason from the client's money
Show them as excluded, with their size and the date they must be ready
questions.why: Work by others is shown as an exclusion so the client knows it is not in the price. Stating the size and date makes clear what must be ready before the carport can be fixed, and protects the shop from delays it did not cause.

questions.q: Why is Rushane's labour rate J$1,450 an hour when the welders' basic pay is J$1,100 an hour?
o: It also covers payroll contributions, holidays and sick pay
It includes a bonus that is paid to the welder when the job ends
It includes the overtime premium for every hour that is worked
It includes the GCT that must be added to every hour of labour
questions.why: Employing someone costs more than the basic wage: the employer's statutory contributions (such as NIS and NHT), holiday and sick pay, and time that cannot be charged to jobs. GCT is added to the final price, not built into the rate.

questions.q: What else must Nordia allow for when she prices the galvanising?
o: Nothing else, as the price per kilogram covers every galvanising cost
Two coats of paint over the zinc, since galvanising must always be painted
Transport to Kingston and back, handling, and the time the steel is away
Extra welding after galvanising, to join the parts that were dipped
questions.why: Galvanisers usually price by the kilogram for the dipping alone. Getting the steel there and back, loading, handling and the days it is away are real costs of the job.

questions.q: How should Nordia's quotation deal with the old concrete base?
o: Ignore it, as the school is responsible for anything under the stand
Add a very large contingency so that any problem with it is covered
Price a new concrete base without telling the school it was included
Check it on the site visit, and state what is assumed and excluded
questions.why: A site visit shows what can be seen; the quotation then states what the price assumes (for example a level, sound base) and what is excluded, so any extra work becomes a priced variation.

questions.q: The school board accepts Nordia's quotation two weeks after it ran out. What should she do?
o: Start at once at the quoted price, since the board has now signed
Re-check the prices, and confirm or revise them in writing
Refuse the job, because a quotation that has run out is cancelled
Add 10% to the price on the final bill without telling the board
questions.why: After the validity period the shop is no longer bound by the price. Imported steel priced in US dollars may cost more now, so prices are checked and the price confirmed or revised in writing before work starts.

questions.q: What price before GCT gives Kimoy's business a 20% margin?
questions.why: For a margin, price = cost ÷ (1 − 0.20) = 480,000 ÷ 0.8 = J$600,000, so the profit of J$120,000 is 20% of the price. Adding 20% to the cost (J$576,000) is a 20% mark-up, which gives only a 16.7% margin.

questions.q: In what order are the figures built up on Kimoy's estimate sheet?
o: Direct costs, then GCT, then overheads and contingency, then profit
Profit first, then direct costs, then overheads, then GCT and contingency
Direct costs, then overheads and contingency, then profit, then GCT
Direct costs, then profit, then GCT, then overheads and contingency
questions.why: Profit is worked out on the total cost, which includes overheads and contingency, and GCT is worked out last on the price before tax and shown as its own line.

questions.q: The manager wants a lower price. Which response is most professional?
o: Keep the galvanised design but use thinner tread plate without saying so
Cut the price by 20% and hope the team works faster on the job
Offer a priced painted option, and explain its shorter life by the sea
Take out the contingency and the profit, and keep the same design
questions.why: An honest alternative lets the client choose with full information. Secretly using thinner steel is dishonest and unsafe, and working at no profit or with no allowance for risk puts the business in danger.

questions.q: Which payment terms are most usual and sensible for this three-week job?
o: The full price paid in advance, before any material is ordered
No deposit, and the whole price invoiced 90 days after completion
Half the price on the first day, and half after a year in use
A deposit on order, a stage payment, and the balance at the end
questions.why: A deposit pays for materials and confirms the order; a stage payment keeps cash coming in while costs are paid out; the balance is due when the work is done. The terms are agreed in writing on the quotation.

questions.q: Besides the extra price, what must Leroy's written variation include?
o: The names of the welders who will do the extra work on the gate
Any change to the completion date, and the client's signed approval
A promise that no other changes will ever be accepted on the job
The original quotation's price for the gate, crossed out and replaced
questions.why: A wider gate and a motor take extra time and materials. The variation states the new work, its price with GCT at the current rate, any new completion date, and is signed before the work is done.

questions.q: Why should Leroy not simply "add it to the bill" at the end?
o: No price has been agreed, so payment could be disputed
The extra work will be done for free, as the quotation was signed
Adding work to a job after it is signed is against the law in Jamaica
Final bills are not allowed to show work that was not on the drawing
questions.why: Without a written, agreed price the client may say the cost is too high or that it was meant to be included. Agreeing it first protects both sides.

questions.q: By what percentage did the labour hours go over Jodian's estimate?
questions.why: The difference is 50 − 40 = 10 hours, and a variance is worked out against the estimate: 10 ÷ 40 = 25%. Dividing by the actual hours (10 ÷ 50 = 20%) uses the wrong figure.

questions.q: Which lesson should Jodian write in her review?
o: Charge the fisherman the extra J$8,000 on top of the agreed price
Add 25% to the labour in every future estimate to be on the safe side
Order steel once the job is confirmed; check lengths before cutting
Leave consumables out of estimates, since they came in under budget
questions.why: The review finds the causes: the steel price rose while she waited, and rework came from a cutting error. Ordering promptly and checking lengths before cutting fixes the causes; the client's agreed price does not change.

questions.q: A shop's overheads are J$5.4 million a year, and it has about 6,000 productive labour hours a year. What overhead rate per hour should it add to its jobs?
questions.why: Overhead rate = yearly overheads ÷ yearly productive hours = 5,400,000 ÷ 6,000 = J$900 an hour. A job of 30 hours would then carry J$27,000 of overheads.

questions.q: A MIG job needs about 4 hours of arc time at a gas flow of 15 litres a minute. About how much shielding gas is used, before any allowance for purging?
o: 7200 litres
3600 litres
900 litres
240 litres
questions.why: Gas used = flow × arc time = 15 litres a minute × 240 minutes = 3600 litres. 900 litres is only one hour of arc time, and 7200 litres would be eight hours.
